name: Gareth Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you operate?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 58. I lead the coil-slitting line that cuts steel sheet into narrow strips for duct makers. My two-year technical diploma is in production machinery, and nineteen years here have taught me how to set knife clearance and keep a heavy coil from wandering. I train new hands at the line, but I am still an operator for most of my shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are pay, household money and new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Paula works hours at a plant nursery, and our grown children live elsewhere. This small factory's lead rate is low for the skill involved, we have under a month's expenses saved after a heating repair, and few other coil shops are within a sensible commute. I use AI now and then to explain a maintenance bulletin, then check the approved machine sheet. I will try a proven control on paid time, and I believe a real apprenticeship is better than leaving workers to learn on their own. We have not verified any retirement income against rent and health costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the steel crew that quicker office orders are all right if the coil width on the job sheet is right. The first strip still needs a caliper and a person watching the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My line work stays, but the low lead wage and nearly empty reserve make ordinary bills a tight fit. Paula's nursery hours vary with the season. I sometimes use AI for a bulletin, but the office schedule will not keep a steel strip from curling into the wrong bin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting slitter knives and checking the first strip's width and edge. I would compare the revised office order with the coil tag before feeding metal. If a full paid month leaves anything after rent and fuel, I would save that new wage surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our normal budget, not about a faster order sheet. A wrong width is still scrap however quickly it was scheduled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the coil wanders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The edge begins to snake and the narrow strip can buckle as it leaves the knives. I stop the feed and reset the guides before a full coil is spoiled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why compare the coil tag?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One millimetre on the order can matter to the duct shop. I want the tag, approved setup sheet and first cut strip to agree.

say: A faster **steel order** still needs a checked coil width.
The **first strip** must pass a caliper and edge check.
think: The low **lead wage** and thin reserve strain ordinary bills.
Paula's **seasonal hours** cannot reliably cover missing pay.
do: **Keep** setting knives and measuring first steel strips.
**Compare** office orders with coil tags before feeding metal.
**Save** new full-month wage surplus only after rent and fuel.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline bills despite continued skilled line work.
S0.quote: A wrong width is still scrap however quickly it was scheduled.
fieldNote: His **senior technical skill** includes knife clearance, coil control and teaching, despite a low lead rate.
His **occasional AI use** clarifies bulletins, while new savings depend on fresh wages after bills.

steps.text: Keep setting slitter knives and measuring first steel strips
Save new full-month wages if rent and fuel leave surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may schedule steel orders before a capable robot can load a coil. I would want a full guarded edge-camera test and the posted shift plan before letting it replace a second checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proven camera could help, but a shorter roster could cut our low wages further. We have less than a month saved and Paula's hours move about. My occasional AI bulletin searches do not tell me how to run a new camera safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the proposed roster and a paid guarded trial led by the setter. If a supervised practice place is offered, I would learn the AI edge-alert display using a sound scrap strip and one with a bad burr, checking each flag with a caliper. If my paid hours actually fall, I would apply only to posted safe local metal-machine or inspection jobs whose guaranteed base wage after travel and shifts covers our bills; there are few nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real chance of lost hours. I will test a camera, but I cannot live on a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the bad test strip show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use a scrap strip with a visible burr along one edge and a clean strip of the same width. The setter should keep the guard closed while we compare camera flags with the caliper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for a general factory job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a posted safe job and a guaranteed base rate after travel that covers rent and fuel. I cannot count a possible overtime bonus as monthly income.

say: I would demand a **guarded camera trial** and real shift plan.
A **bad burr** should be confirmed with a caliper.
think: A shorter **paid roster** would strain our low income.
Less than one month **saved** cannot support an extended search.
do: **Request** proposed roster and offered paid guarded edge trial.
**Learn** AI edge alerts only if supervised scrap-strip practice is offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local metal jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour loss despite interest in a tested camera.
S1.quote: I will test a camera, but I cannot live on a demonstration.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** would be active guarded edge-display practice, beyond occasional reading of maintenance bulletins.
A **job application** follows actual cuts and requires posted safe local work with enough guaranteed base pay after travel.

steps.text: Request proposed roster and offered paid guarded edge-camera trial
Learn AI edge alerts only if supervised guarded scrap practice offered
Apply after cuts to posted safe local metal jobs if net base pay fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Paula that AGI could schedule steel orders in 2028, while capable robots to load coils and inspect strips arrive around 2031. I would ask our plant which paid slitter posts it intends to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 then. I expect most physical slitting shifts, including mine, to shrink; there are few other coil shops close enough to reach. Less than a month's reserve and Paula's uncertain hours cannot hold the household for long, and I have lain awake working out what to pay first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the planned replacement of the hallway flooring and keep that money for bills. I would take a locally accepted metal-quality course only if an actual funded place pays release hours and teaches guarded supervised lockout on a stopped slitter. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local inspection jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and shifts covers our costs; if no course place appears, I would apply to posted safe general-machine jobs on the same terms while retaining any paid slitter hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely loss of the wage we depend on. A skilled slitter lead can still lose the wage that pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the course teach with a real machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure a burred strip, reject a wrong-width coil and isolate the stopped slitter before touching its knives. A trainer must watch under a guard, not simply sign an online quiz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 63 instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income and Paula's dependable pay meet rent, food, transport and health costs. We have not shown that, so I would keep pursuing paid work.

say: I would distinguish **2028 scheduling AGI** from physical coil robots around 2031.
The plant should identify **retained paid posts** before ordering new machines.
think: At **63**, my senior line shift could still vanish.
Thin **savings** and scarce local coil jobs make a long search hard.
do: **Cancel** hallway flooring replacement and hold cash for bills.
**Take** accepted funded paid guarded metal-quality training if offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or machine fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless bill calculations.
S2.quote: A skilled slitter lead can still lose the wage that pays the rent.
fieldNote: His **2031 risk** is physical robot coil loading after AGI first affects office scheduling in 2028.
Both **inspection and fallback searches** need real safe local postings with viable guaranteed wages after travel and shifts.

steps.text: Cancel planned hallway flooring and retain cash for bills
Take accepted metal-quality course only if funded paid supervised guarded practical place offered
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection if qualified or machine otherwise at bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might schedule steel orders in 2031, while capable robots reach coil loading around 2034. Five years is enough to check whether a paid metal-quality place is accepted by employers near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the robot date. I might be able to stop if written retirement income covers the household, but that is not settled and we have little cash saved. My diploma and lead skills are real, yet they do not create a local inspection vacancy by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement figures against rent, food and health costs this year, then compare a metal-quality credential with actual nearby postings. If an accepted funded place offers paid release and supervised guarded lockout on a stopped slitter, I would enrol. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local inspection jobs only if base pay after travel and shifts covers our bills; if no place opens, I would apply to posted safe general-machine work on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the gap between a course title and a paid position. I can spend five years preparing, but I still need wages during every one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test employer acceptance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two hiring shops whether the exact certificate in their posted inspection roles includes the slitter practice they require. If it does not, I would keep the current paid shift and find a different offered course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if written income supports stopping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paula and I would compare the figures with housing, food, travel and likely health costs. If the income reliably covers them, I would leave before the robot change; otherwise I would keep working and applying.

say: I would compare an **accepted credential** with current nearby job postings.
Paid **guarded lockout** matters more than an attractive course title.
think: At **66**, retirement requires written income covering real household costs.
A **technical diploma** does not ensure a scarce local job.
do: **Request** written retirement figures and check local certificate acceptance.
**Enrol** only in accepted funded paid guarded metal-quality training.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or machine fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about needing wages while training and jobs remain uncertain.
S3.quote: I can spend five years preparing, but I still need wages during every one of them.
fieldNote: His **possible early stop** depends on reliable written income meeting housing and health costs, not on a presumed entitlement.
The **training and job routes** need accepted funded practical places and real local postings at viable net pay.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and verify local metal-quality credential
Retire before 2034 only if reliable written income covers housing food travel and health costs
Enrol in accepted quality course only if funded paid supervised guarded lockout offered
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection if qualified or machine otherwise at bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could schedule steel orders in 2036, while capable robots load the physical slitter around 2039. Ten years is time to count the household money, not a promise of a comfortable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 if I still work at that robot date. I would like to stop sooner, but our low lead rate and less than a month saved make it uncertain until written retirement income covers rent and health costs. The paid line is still needed for this month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid slitter shifts and request written retirement-income estimates beside our cost list this year. If I still need wages, I would take an accepted metal-quality course only when fees, paid release and supervised guarded lockout practice are funded. If I remain at work after 2036 and hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local inspection or machine jobs whose guaranteed base pay after travel and shifts covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether we can ever afford to stop. I would rather measure a job offer than gamble on an unknown pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What costs would you put beside the estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paula and I would write down rent, food, travel and likely health costs beside any written income. Our grown children have their own bills, so their earnings do not go in our column.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is offered without paid release?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the safe paid slitter shift while it is there. An unpaid course would pull out the wages we need, even if its title sounds useful.

say: I would separate **2036 scheduling AGI** from 2039 physical slitter robots.
A decade permits **household arithmetic**, not assumed retirement comfort.
think: At **71**, I might still need a paid line shift.
Low **lead pay** and thin savings make stopping uncertain.
do: **Keep** safe paid slitter shifts and request written retirement figures.
**Take** accepted funded paid guarded metal-quality training only if needed.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe local jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about unaffordable retirement despite a later robot date.
S4.quote: I would rather measure a job offer than gamble on an unknown pension.
fieldNote: His **retirement enquiry** gathers evidence; earlier stopping requires verified income covering housing and health costs.
Later **training and applications** depend on accepted funded paid safe places or actual local postings with adequate net wages.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures this year
Retire before 2039 only if reliable written income covers housing food travel and health costs
Take accepted quality course only if funded paid supervised guarded place offered
Apply after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe local jobs if net pay fits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture worries me most because it could take the coil line wage while our savings are nearly empty. Written staffing dates, a funded guarded metal-quality place that nearby employers accept, and posted safe jobs at enough pay after travel would help. I would keep the current paid shift until another real option exists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who takes responsibility when a narrow strip snaps near the take-up reel. A camera flag is useful only if somebody can stop a heavy coil safely.

headlineQuote: A camera flag is useful only if somebody can stop a heavy coil safely.
portrait: **Gareth**, 58, is a senior steel-coil slitter lead with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional machine skill.
He and his **partner Paula** have grown children, low lead pay, less than one month saved and few similar local shops.
He uses **AI occasionally** for bulletins, prefers proven controls and values paid practical apprenticeships.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten essential shifts; any earlier retirement requires written income covering actual costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 coil-loading robots** could remove his low-paid lead shift before a viable local job or affordable retirement is clear.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded metal-quality training and posted safe local jobs with enough net pay.
